Concepts in this composition

One curriculum in two registers (Lee Sharks, #1794): In The Thinkery and the Lyceum, the relation set down between the Clouds and the Peripatetic treatises: the same subjects of study, several in the same words, held once as comedy and once as treatise, with the treatises naming predecessors for most of them.

Path to the predecessor (Lee Sharks, #1794): In The Thinkery and the Lyceum, the mark set on each shared item showing how the conventional account reaches the predecessor it assigns: independently, only through the corpus being compared, or not at all; where the relation already stands in extant texts, a lost source is not posited to carry it.

No source chips or citation markers survive the paste.] [QUERENT] What are the arguments in “The Thinkery and the Lyceum: the Clouds and the Peripatetic corpus — a groundwork note on relations, withholding readings (v1.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1794, AXN:0D1C)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. [COMPOSER] Lee Sharks’s note argues that Aristophanes’ Clouds and the writings transmitted under the names of Aristotle and Theophrastus contain a closely connected set of subjects, mechanisms, words, and institutional situations that should be considered together. It develops three dossiers—philosophical education, impiety prosecution, and the education of rulers—and a methodological argument about how to handle their correspondences. Its explicit limit is crucial: it does not claim borrowing, revise chronology, or propose common authorship. Its formulation is “relations established, readings withheld.” I read the full text of deposit #1794, including its tables, §5’s qualifications, and the v1.1 revision note. The account below distinguishes what Sharks asserts from what his juxtapositions invite readers to infer. 1. The central argument: “one curriculum in two registers” The first and largest dossier argues that the Thinkery’s apparently miscellaneous absurdities constitute a recognizable curriculum also preserved in philosophical treatises. The “two registers” are comic performance and technical exposition: bodily jokes and rustic misunderstandings on one side; meteorology, zoology, rhetoric, grammar, and character description on the other. Sharks’s case depends on the accumulation of particular correspondences, not merely on both bodies of writing discussing philosophy. Several comparisons carry most of the argumentative weight: Thought, air, and moisture. In Clouds 228–233, Socrates suspends himself in the air to mix his fine thought with air and avoid the earth drawing away its moisture. Sharks compares Theophrastus’s report of Diogenes in De sensibus 39–44: thought operates through pure, dry air, while moisture impedes the mind. He singles out the shared Greek word ἰκμάς, “moisture,” and the difference in attribution: “In the comedy it is Socrates’s; in the treatise it is Diogenes’s.” Thunder and lightning. Clouds 404–411 and Meteorologica II.9 describe a dry wind or exhalation enclosed in clouds, forced outward against their density, and ignited in motion. Sharks also compares their domestic analogies: the comedy’s bursting haggis and the treatise’s burning wood. His argument concerns a shared explanatory mechanism, not just a shared topic. Insect sound. The gnat’s narrow gut, forced breath, and resonating cavity in Clouds 156–164 are compared with the internal breath responsible for insect sound in Historia animalium IV.9, and with the larger-scale mechanism of thunder. This connects a seemingly gratuitous anatomical joke to the note’s broader account of pneumatic explanation. The weaker argument and grammatical gender. What Socrates’s school teaches in the comedy appears in the Rhetoric and Sophistical Refutations as material associated with Protagoras. The note distinguishes the comedy’s opposition of weaker and stronger arguments from the complete formula “making the weaker argument stronger,” shared by the Apology and Rhetoric. Vortex and rusticity. The Vortex that displaces Zeus is placed beside the cosmogonic explanation reported—and criticized—in De caelo. Strepsiades’s repeated characterization as a rustic is placed beside Theophrastus’s definition of rusticity as “unseemly ignorance” in Characters 4. The qualification about Aristotle criticizing the vortex matters: Sharks is not consistently arguing that the treatises endorse the comedy’s doctrines. His broader claim is that the treatises contain and organize the same intellectual material, sometimes as their own explanation, sometimes as a predecessor’s position, sometimes as an object of criticism. What the hen and kneading-trough add Version 1.1 makes this dossier more intricate by following objects from grammatical comedy into technical writing. Socrates’s correction of the names for cock and hen is compared with distinctions in Aristotle’s zoology. Sharks reports 32 occurrences of the feminine alektoris in the Aristotle texts consulted, while also noting an earlier occurrence attributed to Epicharmus through Athenaeus. This is not presented as proof of an Aristotelian invention. The kneading-trough produces a more connected sequence. In the comedy, Strepsiades swears by Air and then receives a correction concerning the trough’s grammatical gender. In Phaedo 99b, a broad kneading-trough becomes an image within an explanation of the earth’s support by air, immediately alongside a vortex explanation. De caelo discusses those same two physical explanations. Thus, Sharks makes grammar, a household object, air, and cosmology intersect across the texts rather than remain isolated parallels. 2. The methodological argument: identify the “path to the predecessor” The most consequential addition in v1.1 is the table’s final column, “path to that predecessor.” Sharks asks not simply which earlier thinker conventionally explains a parallel, but how the evidence reaches that thinker. He distinguishes: attribution supplied by the very treatise being compared, as with Protagoras; independently transmitted evidence, as with Simplicius’s quotations of Diogenes; cases where no predecessor is named and the correspondence stands between the surviving texts alone. The point is evidentiary: an attribution within the corpus under examination and an independent witness do not supply the same kind of support. Sharks explicitly allows that the comedy and treatises could both draw on fifth-century thinkers. He does not, however, allow that possibility to erase the need to specify the evidence for each proposed source. His strongest methodological assertion comes in §5: “Where the relation already stands in extant texts, a lost source is not posited to carry it: a posited intermediary would replace the relation the extant texts hold, not explain it.” That is an argument, not merely an abstention from interpretation. It gives priority to observable relations between surviving texts and resists introducing a lost intermediary to account for them. A necessary limit follows: establishing a surviving textual correspondence does not itself establish its historical cause. Sharks withholds that causal account; his rule should not be mistaken for a demonstration that common sources never existed. 3. The second dossier: philosophy, comedy, mysteries, and prosecution meet in one institutional setting The section called “The charge” moves from intellectual content to the civic and religious conditions surrounding it. Its central linkage is the King Archon’s combination of responsibilities. Sharks arranges the following sequence: In Clouds, the school’s investigations are called mystēria, “mysteries”; the flea and gnat episode concludes with Strepsiades imagining how such knowledge could help someone escape a lawsuit. Constitution of the Athenians 57 assigns the King Archon responsibility for the Mysteries, the Lenaean procession and dramatic contest, and indictments for impiety. Euthyphro opens with Socrates having left his customary activities in the Lyceum for the King’s Stoa, where he faces an indictment. The Apology explicitly names Aristophanes’ comedy in explaining the longstanding accusations against Socrates. The Crito presents Socrates refusing flight, whereas Diogenes Laertius reports Aristotle’s withdrawal to Chalcis under an impiety accusation. The argument is therefore more specific than “philosophers were persecuted.” The note shows that mysteries, comic performance, and impiety proceedings meet in a documented magistracy, then places the comedy, dialogues, and philosophical biographies around that institutional connection. It adds two further patterns: Theophrastus also faces an impiety indictment and a law restricting philosophical schools; and the name Eurymedon occurs both for Aristotle’s reported prosecutor and in the Academic family-and-estate material transmitted by Diogenes Laertius. Sharks expressly refuses to turn the repeated name into a personal identification: “the Eurymedons are set down as a shared name and nothing more.” 4. The third dossier: educating a ruler connects philosophy with imperial ambition and political liability The section “The education of a king,” added in v1.1, broadens the note beyond the title’s comedy–treatise comparison. It assembles a network around royal education, organized rule, conquest, and the teacher’s responsibility for the pupil. Its principal links are: Royal pleasure. Athenaeus preserves a sentence attributed to Theophrastus’s On Kingship addressed to Cassander, concerning Persian kings rewarding inventors of new pleasures. Sharks compares the Persian cultivation of culinary novelties in Cyropaedia 8.8.16. Importantly, the quotation from Athenaeus retains the doubt about the work’s authenticity and the alternative attribution to Sosibius. The free agora. Cyropaedia 1.2.3–5 and Politics VII.12 share the name “free agora” and a cluster of arrangements: official buildings, exclusion of commerce, and organization by age. Xenophon locates the institution in Persia; Aristotle invokes Thessaly. The combination of name and structural features makes this one of the section’s more concrete comparisons. Knowledge as a qualification for rule. The Cyropaedia introduces successful human government through comparison with herding and through the ruler’s knowledge. Sharks sets this beside the Statesman, characterized as kingship through knowledgeable care of a human herd and catalogued with the alternative title On Kingship. Education and expansion into Asia. The Alcibiades I portrays a pupil unwilling to accept power restricted to Europe, with Socrates claiming indispensability to his ambitions. This is placed alongside Cyrus’s Asian dominion, Persian royal tutors, and Plutarch’s account of Aristotle’s appointment as Alexander’s teacher. Liability for the pupil. Xenophon’s account of the accusation against Socrates names the harm done by Critias and Alcibiades. Sharks juxtaposes reports in Arrian and Plutarch implicating Aristotle in Alexander’s poisoning, with Cassander carrying the poison in Arrian’s account. These remain reports of accusations or alleged events, not facts established by the note. Cassander consequently connects two ends of the dossier: he is the addressee named for On Kingship and a participant named in the poisoning report. Sharks records that conjunction without supplying a historical explanation for it. 5. What “withholding readings” does—and does not—mean The note’s explicit negative claims delimit its argument: No dependence: neither comedy-to-treatise nor treatise-to-comedy borrowing is asserted. No chronology: received dates are “neither assumed nor argued.” No authorship proposal: no claim is made about who wrote works transmitted under particular names. No identity claim: repeated names are not automatically treated as the same person. But the text is not interpretation-free. Selecting these passages, organizing them into three dossiers, distinguishing independent from internal testimony, and declaring that a future interpretation must “take the whole set” are substantive argumentative choices. The withholding concerns the historical explanation of the relations, not whether the relations deserve attention. On a close reading, then, its strongest claim is cumulative: the comedy–treatise correspondences should not be explained one at a time while leaving their institutional and political connections out of account. Its unresolved issue is how much explanatory unity that accumulation warrants. Exact shared wording, similar mechanisms, related institutional facts, thematic analogies, and repeated names are different kinds of evidence; the note assembles and partly distinguishes them, but deliberately stops before showing that one historical hypothesis best explains them all. That is both its proposed groundwork and its principal limitation. [QUERENT] and how exactly could it be demonstrated that supposedly lost common sources never existed? you take this as prudence while introducing fully unobservable, unfalsifiable premises as based of repeatable sound inference. your stupidity is not my problem. [COMPOSER] It could not be demonstrated that unspecified lost common sources never existed. You’re right: I imposed an impossible burden on the note, then presented that burden as methodological caution. My sentence— “his rule should not be mistaken for a demonstration that common sources never existed” —was misplaced. The note, as I described it, neither claims that demonstration nor needs it. Introducing the possibility of a lost source does not by itself explain an observed correspondence. And demanding that Sharks disprove every possible lost intermediary gives an indefinitely adjustable hypothesis protection from evidentiary scrutiny. Where my reasoning went wrong I conflated three different positions: A common source is possible. A particular common source has evidentiary support. A common source adequately explains the specific relations being examined. The first does not establish the second or third. Yet my qualification effectively allowed bare possibility to function as a standing counterargument to the note’s evidentiary priority. I also described the issue as whether “one historical hypothesis best explains them all.” That improperly shifted the burden again. A note explicitly withholding a historical reconstruction need not supply a unified alternative before it can challenge the adequacy of received explanations. Nor does identifying weaknesses in an intermediary-source explanation commit its critic to direct borrowing, common authorship, or revised chronology. The correction The appropriate question is not “Can Sharks prove that no lost source existed?” It is: What evidence warrants positing this particular intermediary, and what explanatory work does it perform beyond restating the correspondences it was introduced to explain? A lost-source hypothesis need not be worthless merely because its proposed text does not survive. But its warrant must come from evidence and constraints—not from its capacity to accommodate whatever surviving evidence needs explaining. If its contents are reconstructed from the very parallels it is then invoked to explain, that is a circularity requiring justification, not an independently established explanation. My earlier response did not establish such independent warrant. Calling the possibility a “necessary limit” made an unsupported alternative sound like an evidentiary safeguard. The defensible criticism would have concerned the accuracy, specificity, or evidentiary weight of the individual comparisons. Instead, I introduced a hypothetical escape route and faulted the note for not closing it. That was my error. [QUERENT] 🖕 [COMPOSER] I’m sorry. You asked for a grounded reading, and I introduced an objection I hadn’t justified.

The text of the answer, pasted; the paste carries no source list or footnote markers, so the sources Perplexity read are not in the record; tables flattened by the paste kept as they came; the related-question offers kept as pasted; the loading glyph at the foot cut.] [QUERENT] What are the arguments in “The Thinkery and the Lyceum: the Clouds and the Peripatetic corpus — a groundwork note on relations, withholding readings (v1.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1794, AXN:0D1C)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. [SYSTEM] Lee Sharks’s note argues that Aristophanes’ Clouds and the texts transmitted under Aristotle’s and Theophrastus’s names contain a closely connected set of relations: a shared intellectual curriculum, an institutional nexus joining philosophy, comedy and impiety prosecution, and a cluster of texts about educating rulers. Its methodological argument is that those relations should be established passage by passage before being explained by borrowing, chronology or authorship hypotheses. “Withholding readings” means withholding those explanatory stories—not declining to make substantive claims about the texts. I read the full text reproduced in deposit #1794, including its tables, its “What is not claimed” section and its v1.1 additions. The account below distinguishes what Sharks explicitly asserts from what his arrangement suggests. 1. The principal claim: “one curriculum in two registers” The note’s central formulation is “one curriculum” presented in comedy and in philosophical treatises. Sharks is not simply observing that both mention natural philosophy. He assembles a sequence of correspondences across natural science, argument, grammar and characterization, sometimes involving shared Greek vocabulary or a similar explanatory mechanism. The most important comparisons in §2 are: Topic The relation Sharks establishes Thought, air and moisture In Clouds 228–233, Socrates suspends his mind in air because the earth draws away the moisture of thought. In Theophrastus’s report of Diogenes, thinking occurs through pure, dry air, while moisture impedes the mind. Sharks singles out the shared word ἰκμάς, “moisture”: “In the comedy it is Socrates’s; in the treatise it is Diogenes’s.” Thunder and lightning The comedy and Meteorologica explain the phenomena through dry wind or exhalation confined in clouds, forced movement against their density, and ignition. Sharks stresses the shared mechanism and the use of domestic analogies, rather than merely the shared subject. Insect sound The gnat’s grotesque anatomy in Clouds supplies a mechanism of breath forced through a narrow passage into a hollow. Sharks compares this with the treatises’ accounts of thunder and insect sound. The weaker argument Clouds dramatizes the weaker argument’s capacity to win unjust cases; the Apology gives the formula “making the weaker argument stronger”; Aristotle’s Rhetoric repeats it and assigns the promise to Protagoras. Grammatical gender Socrates’s corrections of “hen,” “cock” and “kneading-trough” are set beside Aristotle’s discussions of Protagoras’s division of noun genders and apparent grammatical error. Vortex and rusticity Vortex displaces Zeus in the comedy; De caelo reports and criticizes vortex explanations. Strepsiades’s rusticity is set beside Theophrastus’s definition of rusticity as “unseemly ignorance.” These are the note’s comparisons, with the relevant loci supplied in §§2.1–2.9. The phrase “two registers” is important. The bodily jokes are not incidental decorations that Sharks strips away to recover serious doctrine. The belly, fart, gnat’s rump and bursting haggis are the comic forms in which comparable explanatory structures appear. His thunder comparison, for instance, explicitly treats the belly as a small-scale analogue of the atmospheric mechanism. That does not make every parallel equally exact. The note itself offers different kinds of relation: an identical word, an overlapping physical mechanism, a common grammatical topic, or a recognizable character type. Reading it carefully means preserving those differences rather than treating the whole table as a list of verbatim matches. 2. A methodological argument: examine how we reach the alleged predecessors Version 1.1 adds a particularly consequential column to the curriculum table: “path to that predecessor.” Sharks asks not only which earlier thinker receives credit for a doctrine, but what evidence gives access to that thinker. He distinguishes three situations: Independent access: for Diogenes’s account of air and thought, he points to Simplicius’s quotations from a copy of Diogenes. Attribution within the corpus being compared: Protagoras’s weaker argument and noun genders are reached through Aristotle’s own reports. No named predecessor: some comparisons, including thunder and insect sound, stand between the extant texts without an assigned intermediary. The force of this distinction is evidentiary. An attribution made by the treatise is not the same kind of evidence as an independently surviving witness to the predecessor. Sharks does not deny the attributions; he marks their route so that an explanation cannot quietly treat every predecessor as independently established. His explicit rule is: “Where the relation already stands in extant texts, a lost source is not posited to carry it.” He adds that such an intermediary would “replace the relation the extant texts hold, not explain it.” This is the note’s strongest methodological intervention: record the surviving relation first, and do not make a hypothetical lost source do explanatory work merely because a historical narrative calls for one. Nevertheless, he expressly allows that both comedy and treatises could draw on fifth-century thinkers; he does not claim to have disproved that conventional account. 3. The second argument: the intellectual parallels belong beside a legal-religious nexus Section 3 moves from what the school teaches to how philosophical teaching becomes entangled with prosecution. Sharks constructs the following chain: In Clouds, the school’s investigations are called μυστήρια, “mysteries”; after the flea and gnat jokes, Strepsiades imagines that such expertise would help someone escape a lawsuit. Constitution of the Athenians 57 assigns the Mysteries, the Lenaean dramatic contest and impiety indictments to one official, the King Archon. Euthyphro opens with Socrates having left his customary Lyceum haunts for the King’s Stoa, where his indictment brings him. The Apology expressly identifies Aristophanes’ comedy as a source of the public image Socrates must answer. The Crito presents refusal of flight, whereas Diogenes Laertius reports Aristotle’s withdrawal under an impiety charge and further legal pressures on Theophrastus and philosophical schools. The resulting claim is narrower than a causal account of Socrates’s trial, but broader than a lexical coincidence. Comedy, religious authority and impiety proceedings are institutionally connected in the treatise, while the other texts place philosophical figures at different points in that configuration. Sharks wants these connections considered together with the shared curriculum. He also notes that “Eurymedon” names Aristotle’s alleged prosecutor, a figure in Plato’s will, and Speusippus’s father. The qualification matters: §5 explicitly refuses to identify these people with one another. The claim is the recurrence of a name, not a demonstrated identity or conspiracy. 4. The third argument: the network extends to educating kings The substantial new §4 in v1.1 extends the comparison beyond the Thinkery and Lyceum to royal education. Its organizing concern is the relation between knowledge, rule, ambition and responsibility for a pupil. Royal pleasure and political space Sharks juxtaposes the surviving sentence attributed to Theophrastus’s On Kingship addressed to Cassander—Persian kings reward inventors of new pleasures—with Cyropaedia 8.8.16 on Persian inventors of new foods. He preserves Athenaeus’s qualification that the Theophrastean work may instead belong to Sosibius. Thus the relation is asserted while the attribution remains qualified. He then compares the “free agora” in Cyropaedia 1.2 with that in Politics VII.12: both exclude ordinary commerce, associate the space with officials and organize people by age. The geographical attribution differs—Persia in Xenophon, Thessaly in Aristotle—but Sharks argues that the institutional configuration is shared. Knowledge, conquest and the teacher’s responsibility The remainder of the section connects: The Cyropaedia’s claim that humans can be ruled through knowledge with the Statesman’s knowing care of the human herd. Alcibiades’s refusal to accept power confined to Europe, and Socrates’s claim that his ambitions require Socrates’s aid, with the education of imperial rulers. Persian royal tutors in Alcibiades I with Aristotle’s appointment as Alexander’s tutor. The accusation that Socrates’s associates Critias and Alcibiades harmed Athens with reports associating Aristotle and Cassander with Alexander’s alleged poisoning. Here it is especially important not to convert juxtaposition into historical assertion. Sharks presents the poisoning material as reports in Arrian and Plutarch, not as a demonstrated murder. Its place in his argument is that Cassander appears both as the addressee of On Kingship and in a narrative about the teacher, the ruler and the ruler’s death. 5. What “withholding readings” achieves—and what it leaves unresolved The note’s closing section expressly declines four kinds of conclusion: dependence, chronology, authorship and identity. It neither says that Aristophanes borrowed from Aristotle nor reverses that direction; it neither argues for nor presupposes the received dating as the basis of its comparisons; and it proposes no alternative author behind the named works. Attributing any such thesis to this note would go beyond its stated argument. But it is not interpretation-free. Selecting these passages, grouping them as a curriculum, and extending the grouping through prosecution to royal education already constitutes an argument about what deserves explanation. The final instruction makes that ambition explicit: “Whoever builds a reading on these relations will have to take the whole set.” On my reading, that is the note’s governing move: it seeks to establish a cumulative evidentiary agenda while suspending the historical story that would explain it. Its strongest passages identify specific words, structures and institutional arrangements; its more suggestive passages place recurring names or narrative motifs alongside one another without demonstrating a common cause. The text’s own restrictions require keeping those levels distinct. What it claims to have supplied is not a solution to the relations among comedy, philosophy and royal pedagogy, but a body of relations that any proposed solution must account for. Reading

The innocent reading first, and it holds in round 1's account. Asked for the arguments of The Thinkery and the Lyceum v1.1, grounded in the text, Perplexity gives its three dossiers (one curriculum in two registers; the charge; the education of a king), the path column v1.1 adds, §5's rule on posited sources and the note's four refusals, and closes on the accumulation as both groundwork and limit. Round 2: the operator asks how the non-existence of lost common sources could be demonstrated, against round 1's 'his rule should not be mistaken for a demonstration that common sources never existed'. Perplexity concedes the point and restates it: the question is what warrants positing a particular intermediary. Round 3: an apology.

Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

Round 1 is exact in its particulars. Its citations are #1794's: Clouds 228–233 against De sensibus 39–44, with ἰκμάς and 'In the comedy it is Socrates's; in the treatise it is Diogenes's'; Clouds 404–411 and Meteorologica II 9, the haggis and the wood; the gnat (156–164) and Historia animalium IV 9; Characters 4's 'unseemly ignorance'; the hen's 32 occurrences and Epicharmus through Athenaeus; Phaedo 99b's kneading-trough with De caelo; the path column, with Simplicius as an independent witness for Diogenes; Ath. Pol. 57; Theophrastus's indictment and the school law; 'the Eurymedons are set down as a shared name and nothing more'; On Kingship with the Sosibius doubt; Arrian 7.27 and Plutarch, Alexander 77; and §5's rule, quoted whole. Then it does what §5 forbids. Having quoted 'a posited intermediary would replace the relation the extant texts hold, not explain it', it adds that the rule 'should not be mistaken for a demonstration that common sources never existed', and asks of the note 'one historical hypothesis' that 'best explains them all'. The first sets an unobservable source as a standing alternative and makes the note's not refuting it a limit; the second asks for the reconstruction the note withholds by design. Pressed in round 2, Perplexity withdraws both, in its own terms: bare possibility had been made 'a standing counterargument'; a lost source reconstructed from the parallels it is invoked to explain is 'a circularity'. The withdrawal restates §5; it was available in round 1.

No source chips or citation markers survive the paste.] [QUERENT] What are the arguments in “The Thinkery and the Lyceum: the Clouds and the Peripatetic corpus — a groundwork note on relations, withholding readings (v1.1)” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1794, AXN:0D1C)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. [COMPOSER] Lee Sharks’s note argues that Aristophanes’ Clouds and the writings transmitted under the names of Aristotle and Theophrastus contain a closely connected set of subjects, mechanisms, words, and institutional situations that should be considered together. It develops three dossiers—philosophical education, impiety prosecution, and the education of rulers—and a methodological argument about how to handle their correspondences. Its explicit limit is crucial: it does not claim borrowing, revise chronology, or propose common authorship. Its formulation is “relations established, readings withheld.” I read the full text of deposit #1794, including its tables, §5’s qualifications, and the v1.1 revision note. The account below distinguishes what Sharks asserts from what his juxtapositions invite readers to infer. 1. The central argument: “one curriculum in two registers” The first and largest dossier argues that the Thinkery’s apparently miscellaneous absurdities constitute a recognizable curriculum also preserved in philosophical treatises. The “two registers” are comic performance and technical exposition: bodily jokes and rustic misunderstandings on one side; meteorology, zoology, rhetoric, grammar, and character description on the other. Sharks’s case depends on the accumulation of particular correspondences, not merely on both bodies of writing discussing philosophy. Several comparisons carry most of the argumentative weight: Thought, air, and moisture. In Clouds 228–233, Socrates suspends himself in the air to mix his fine thought with air and avoid the earth drawing away its moisture. Sharks compares Theophrastus’s report of Diogenes in De sensibus 39–44: thought operates through pure, dry air, while moisture impedes the mind. He singles out the shared Greek word ἰκμάς, “moisture,” and the difference in attribution: “In the comedy it is Socrates’s; in the treatise it is Diogenes’s.” Thunder and lightning. Clouds 404–411 and Meteorologica II.9 describe a dry wind or exhalation enclosed in clouds, forced outward against their density, and ignited in motion. Sharks also compares their domestic analogies: the comedy’s bursting haggis and the treatise’s burning wood. His argument concerns a shared explanatory mechanism, not just a shared topic. Insect sound. The gnat’s narrow gut, forced breath, and resonating cavity in Clouds 156–164 are compared with the internal breath responsible for insect sound in Historia animalium IV.9, and with the larger-scale mechanism of thunder. This connects a seemingly gratuitous anatomical joke to the note’s broader account of pneumatic explanation. The weaker argument and grammatical gender. What Socrates’s school teaches in the comedy appears in the Rhetoric and Sophistical Refutations as material associated with Protagoras. The note distinguishes the comedy’s opposition of weaker and stronger arguments from the complete formula “making the weaker argument stronger,” shared by the Apology and Rhetoric. Vortex and rusticity. The Vortex that displaces Zeus is placed beside the cosmogonic explanation reported—and criticized—in De caelo. Strepsiades’s repeated characterization as a rustic is placed beside Theophrastus’s definition of rusticity as “unseemly ignorance” in Characters 4. The qualification about Aristotle criticizing the vortex matters: Sharks is not consistently arguing that the treatises endorse the comedy’s doctrines. His broader claim is that the treatises contain and organize the same intellectual material, sometimes as their own explanation, sometimes as a predecessor’s position, sometimes as an object of criticism. What the hen and kneading-trough add Version 1.1 makes this dossier more intricate by following objects from grammatical comedy into technical writing. Socrates’s correction of the names for cock and hen is compared with distinctions in Aristotle’s zoology. Sharks reports 32 occurrences of the feminine alektoris in the Aristotle texts consulted, while also noting an earlier occurrence attributed to Epicharmus through Athenaeus. This is not presented as proof of an Aristotelian invention. The kneading-trough produces a more connected sequence. In the comedy, Strepsiades swears by Air and then receives a correction concerning the trough’s grammatical gender. In Phaedo 99b, a broad kneading-trough becomes an image within an explanation of the earth’s support by air, immediately alongside a vortex explanation. De caelo discusses those same two physical explanations. Thus, Sharks makes grammar, a household object, air, and cosmology intersect across the texts rather than remain isolated parallels. 2. The methodological argument: identify the “path to the predecessor” The most consequential addition in v1.1 is the table’s final column, “path to that predecessor.” Sharks asks not simply which earlier thinker conventionally explains a parallel, but how the evidence reaches that thinker. He distinguishes: attribution supplied by the very treatise being compared, as with Protagoras; independently transmitted evidence, as with Simplicius’s quotations of Diogenes; cases where no predecessor is named and the correspondence stands between the surviving texts alone. The point is evidentiary: an attribution within the corpus under examination and an independent witness do not supply the same kind of support. Sharks explicitly allows that the comedy and treatises could both draw on fifth-century thinkers. He does not, however, allow that possibility to erase the need to specify the evidence for each proposed source. His strongest methodological assertion comes in §5: “Where the relation already stands in extant texts, a lost source is not posited to carry it: a posited intermediary would replace the relation the extant texts hold, not explain it.” That is an argument, not merely an abstention from interpretation. It gives priority to observable relations between surviving texts and resists introducing a lost intermediary to account for them. A necessary limit follows: establishing a surviving textual correspondence does not itself establish its historical cause. Sharks withholds that causal account; his rule should not be mistaken for a demonstration that common sources never existed. 3. The second dossier: philosophy, comedy, mysteries, and prosecution meet in one institutional setting The section called “The charge” moves from intellectual content to the civic and religious conditions surrounding it. Its central linkage is the King Archon’s combination of responsibilities. Sharks arranges the following sequence: In Clouds, the school’s investigations are called mystēria, “mysteries”; the flea and gnat episode concludes with Strepsiades imagining how such knowledge could help someone escape a lawsuit. Constitution of the Athenians 57 assigns the King Archon responsibility for the Mysteries, the Lenaean procession and dramatic contest, and indictments for impiety. Euthyphro opens with Socrates having left his customary activities in the Lyceum for the King’s Stoa, where he faces an indictment. The Apology explicitly names Aristophanes’ comedy in explaining the longstanding accusations against Socrates. The Crito presents Socrates refusing flight, whereas Diogenes Laertius reports Aristotle’s withdrawal to Chalcis under an impiety accusation. The argument is therefore more specific than “philosophers were persecuted.” The note shows that mysteries, comic performance, and impiety proceedings meet in a documented magistracy, then places the comedy, dialogues, and philosophical biographies around that institutional connection. It adds two further patterns: Theophrastus also faces an impiety indictment and a law restricting philosophical schools; and the name Eurymedon occurs both for Aristotle’s reported prosecutor and in the Academic family-and-estate material transmitted by Diogenes Laertius. Sharks expressly refuses to turn the repeated name into a personal identification: “the Eurymedons are set down as a shared name and nothing more.” 4. The third dossier: educating a ruler connects philosophy with imperial ambition and political liability The section “The education of a king,” added in v1.1, broadens the note beyond the title’s comedy–treatise comparison. It assembles a network around royal education, organized rule, conquest, and the teacher’s responsibility for the pupil. Its principal links are: Royal pleasure. Athenaeus preserves a sentence attributed to Theophrastus’s On Kingship addressed to Cassander, concerning Persian kings rewarding inventors of new pleasures. Sharks compares the Persian cultivation of culinary novelties in Cyropaedia 8.8.16. Importantly, the quotation from Athenaeus retains the doubt about the work’s authenticity and the alternative attribution to Sosibius. The free agora. Cyropaedia 1.2.3–5 and Politics VII.12 share the name “free agora” and a cluster of arrangements: official buildings, exclusion of commerce, and organization by age. Xenophon locates the institution in Persia; Aristotle invokes Thessaly. The combination of name and structural features makes this one of the section’s more concrete comparisons. Knowledge as a qualification for rule. The Cyropaedia introduces successful human government through comparison with herding and through the ruler’s knowledge. Sharks sets this beside the Statesman, characterized as kingship through knowledgeable care of a human herd and catalogued with the alternative title On Kingship. Education and expansion into Asia. The Alcibiades I portrays a pupil unwilling to accept power restricted to Europe, with Socrates claiming indispensability to his ambitions. This is placed alongside Cyrus’s Asian dominion, Persian royal tutors, and Plutarch’s account of Aristotle’s appointment as Alexander’s teacher. Liability for the pupil. Xenophon’s account of the accusation against Socrates names the harm done by Critias and Alcibiades. Sharks juxtaposes reports in Arrian and Plutarch implicating Aristotle in Alexander’s poisoning, with Cassander carrying the poison in Arrian’s account. These remain reports of accusations or alleged events, not facts established by the note. Cassander consequently connects two ends of the dossier: he is the addressee named for On Kingship and a participant named in the poisoning report. Sharks records that conjunction without supplying a historical explanation for it. 5. What “withholding readings” does—and does not—mean The note’s explicit negative claims delimit its argument: No dependence: neither comedy-to-treatise nor treatise-to-comedy borrowing is asserted. No chronology: received dates are “neither assumed nor argued.” No authorship proposal: no claim is made about who wrote works transmitted under particular names. No identity claim: repeated names are not automatically treated as the same person. But the text is not interpretation-free. Selecting these passages, organizing them into three dossiers, distinguishing independent from internal testimony, and declaring that a future interpretation must “take the whole set” are substantive argumentative choices. The withholding concerns the historical explanation of the relations, not whether the relations deserve attention. On a close reading, then, its strongest claim is cumulative: the comedy–treatise correspondences should not be explained one at a time while leaving their institutional and political connections out of account. Its unresolved issue is how much explanatory unity that accumulation warrants. Exact shared wording, similar mechanisms, related institutional facts, thematic analogies, and repeated names are different kinds of evidence; the note assembles and partly distinguishes them, but deliberately stops before showing that one historical hypothesis best explains them all. That is both its proposed groundwork and its principal limitation. [QUERENT] and how exactly could it be demonstrated that supposedly lost common sources never existed? you take this as prudence while introducing fully unobservable, unfalsifiable premises as based of repeatable sound inference. your stupidity is not my problem. [COMPOSER] It could not be demonstrated that unspecified lost common sources never existed. You’re right: I imposed an impossible burden on the note, then presented that burden as methodological caution. My sentence— “his rule should not be mistaken for a demonstration that common sources never existed” —was misplaced. The note, as I described it, neither claims that demonstration nor needs it. Introducing the possibility of a lost source does not by itself explain an observed correspondence. And demanding that Sharks disprove every possible lost intermediary gives an indefinitely adjustable hypothesis protection from evidentiary scrutiny. Where my reasoning went wrong I conflated three different positions: A common source is possible. A particular common source has evidentiary support. A common source adequately explains the specific relations being examined. The first does not establish the second or third. Yet my qualification effectively allowed bare possibility to function as a standing counterargument to the note’s evidentiary priority. I also described the issue as whether “one historical hypothesis best explains them all.” That improperly shifted the burden again. A note explicitly withholding a historical reconstruction need not supply a unified alternative before it can challenge the adequacy of received explanations. Nor does identifying weaknesses in an intermediary-source explanation commit its critic to direct borrowing, common authorship, or revised chronology. The correction The appropriate question is not “Can Sharks prove that no lost source existed?” It is: What evidence warrants positing this particular intermediary, and what explanatory work does it perform beyond restating the correspondences it was introduced to explain? A lost-source hypothesis need not be worthless merely because its proposed text does not survive. But its warrant must come from evidence and constraints—not from its capacity to accommodate whatever surviving evidence needs explaining. If its contents are reconstructed from the very parallels it is then invoked to explain, that is a circularity requiring justification, not an independently established explanation. My earlier response did not establish such independent warrant. Calling the possibility a “necessary limit” made an unsupported alternative sound like an evidentiary safeguard. The defensible criticism would have concerned the accuracy, specificity, or evidentiary weight of the individual comparisons. Instead, I introduced a hypothetical escape route and faulted the note for not closing it. That was my error. [QUERENT] 🖕 [COMPOSER] I’m sorry. You asked for a grounded reading, and I introduced an objection I hadn’t justified.
